Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need you to turn this into a clear prompt for a practical community library repair plan for the board to review. the library is Cedar Lane Community Library, at 18 Alder Street, and the prompt should ask for a phased plan based only on the meeting notes below. Address the plan to Leonie, not Ellis. Keep the plan focused on repairs and next steps for these specific issues; this is not a request for a general building-maintenance policy or a public announcement. The notes are mixed with my directions, so put them in a useful order and retain all their details inside the prompt rather than turning them into a short summary.

The notes are from the May 14, 2025 meeting, held in the library reading room from 6:30 to 7:25 pm. Eleven people attended. Mara Chen chaired. The library's usual hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 10 am to 6 pm. We did not decide a repair date or approve hiring anyone. Please make those limits clear. We want the board to be able to see what is known, what could be done next, and what still needs checking; don't write as though a proposal has already been approved or work has already happened.

Here are the actual conditions that were discussed. At the west entrance, the ramp handrail is loose and two screws are missing. No one checked the condition of the material under the screws, so we do not know whether the existing holes will hold replacement fasteners. Near the reading-room skylight there is a water stain after rain on May 9. Nobody saw an active drip during the meeting, so the stain is observed but the source and current status are not established. The archive cabinet needs to stay dry. A folding table has been moved beneath the stain for now, but we didn't decide whether that is a suitable ongoing measure. In the children's room, the sink's cold tap drips and the hot tap works. The shutoff under the sink is hard to reach because supply boxes are stored in front of it. The rear courtyard gate latch sticks when it is damp; nobody reported a security failure. Please don't blend the four issues together as if they had the same cause or urgency.

One person read the following message from Rook & Pine Facilities: “The visit fee is $85. Materials and roof access are not included. This estimate is valid through June 10.” The group has not booked a visit or accepted the estimate. Keep the amount, exclusions, company name, and validity date intact, and distinguish that estimate from any future costs, which are not in the notes. The repair reserve for this phase is capped at $900. That ceiling came up in discussion but does not mean permission to spend it, and no one agreed that the estimate should be paid from it. We need a plan that leaves a decision with the board rather than claiming there is authorization.

Omar said he can look at the ramp on Wednesday mornings. He is a volunteer, not a qualified contractor, and the notes don't say that he has inspected it yet. A possible first step is to ask him to look at it, but don't present that as something already completed or as a professional safety assessment. The library remains open during its usual hours. People mentioned that work in the children's room should be arranged so children are not exposed to a work area, but nobody set a date or a detailed closure arrangement. Thursday after closing was raised as a possible time to discuss, not agreed as a schedule. Keep that distinction; do not turn a suggestion into a booking.

For the skylight stain, we have no inspection findings, no confirmed leak, and no roof-access arrangement. The table is already beneath it, as noted, and the archive cabinet must remain dry. Ask the board or the appropriate person to determine what inspection or other next step is needed. Do not say that the roof is repaired, that the stain has stopped, or that the table resolves the issue. For the sink, the blocked access to the shutoff is relevant to deciding what to check first. For the gate, the sticking happens when damp; the meeting did not establish a failure to secure the courtyard. Keep these points attributed to the notes, not upgraded into conclusions.

The discussion ended with a vote: seven in favor and two opposed to requesting quotes, with two abstentions. That vote was to request quotes; it was not a vote to hire a contractor or approve work. The board's next meeting is June 12. The prompt should ask for a usable plan that can be considered there, including sensible phases, who might need to make or confirm each decision, and open questions where information is missing. Keep names and roles as given, and don't invent a board decision, a contractor, a repair method, prices, inspection results, or a date for the work.

Please make the resulting plan easy to scan, with an opening that states its purpose, a numbered section if it helps distinguish the repair issues or phases, and a final section that identifies the outstanding decisions for the June 12 meeting. Preserve the exact quote above and the distinction between reported conditions, suggestions, and decisions. The plan should be specific enough to guide discussion, but should not give technical directions unsupported by the notes or imply that a volunteer can certify safety. There is no need to add a general introduction to library maintenance. ## Meeting context
The notes are from the May 14, 2025 meeting in the library reading room, held from 6:30 to 7:25 pm. Eleven people attended, and Mara Chen chaired. The library's usual hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 10 am to 6 pm. No repair date was decided, and no one approved hiring anyone.

## Repair issues and reported conditions

1. **West entrance ramp handrail:** The handrail is loose, and two screws are missing. No one checked the material beneath the screws, so it is not known whether the existing holes will hold replacement fasteners. Omar said he can look at the ramp on Wednesday mornings. He is a volunteer, not a qualified contractor, and the notes do not say that he has inspected it. You may identify asking him to look as a possible first step, but do not present it as completed or as a professional safety assessment.

2. **Reading-room skylight:** There is a water stain near the skylight after rain on May 9. Nobody saw an active drip during the meeting, so the source and current status are not established. There are no inspection findings, confirmed leak, or roof-access arrangement. The archive cabinet needs to stay dry. A folding table has been moved beneath the stain, but the group did not decide whether that is a suitable ongoing measure. Ask the board or appropriate person to determine what inspection or other next step is needed. Do not state that the roof is repaired, the stain has stopped, or the table resolves the issue.

3. **Children's-room sink:** The cold tap drips; the hot tap works. Supply boxes in front of the under-sink shutoff make it hard to reach. Keep this access issue in view when identifying what might need to be checked first. People said work in the children's room should be arranged so children are not exposed to a work area, but no date or detailed closure arrangement was set.

4. **Rear courtyard gate:** The latch sticks when it is damp. Nobody reported a security failure. Do not present sticking as proof that the gate has failed to secure the courtyard.

Keep the four issues distinct rather than treating them as if they have the same cause or urgency. Attribute reported conditions to the notes and do not turn them into unsupported conclusions.

## Estimate, reserve, and possible scheduling
One person read this message from Rook & Pine Facilities: “The visit fee is $85. Materials and roof access are not included. This estimate is valid through June 10.” The group has not booked a visit or accepted the estimate. Preserve the company name, amount, exclusions, and validity date, and distinguish the estimate from future costs, which are not given in the notes.

The repair reserve for this phase is capped at $900. This ceiling was discussed but is not permission to spend it, and no one agreed that the estimate should be paid from it. Leave spending and hiring decisions with the board. The library remains open during its usual hours. Thursday after closing was mentioned as a possible time to discuss, not agreed as a work schedule. Do not convert that suggestion into a booking or a date.

## Decisions, phases, and open questions
The discussion ended with a vote of seven in favor and two opposed to requesting quotes, with two abstentions. The vote was to request quotes, not to hire a contractor or approve work. Do not invent a board decision, contractor, repair method, price, inspection result, or work date. Present sensible phases, identify who might need to make or confirm each decision, and note unanswered questions without supplying answers. Do not give technical directions unsupported by the notes or imply that a volunteer can certify safety.

The plan should be easy to scan, begin by stating its purpose, and use a numbered section if helpful for distinguishing the issues or phases. End with distinct information about the outstanding choices for the board's next meeting on June 12, rather than repeating the opening.
